Distaff
DIS-taf
n. (the staff that holds the unspun wool or flax for spinning)
Old English distaef, from a root meaning a bunch of flax, and staef, a staff. It is the stick that carries the raw fibre while the spindle twists it into thread, and in the Authorized Version it appears once, in the hands of the virtuous woman of Proverbs 31.

Biblical Definition

She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff. The verse is one line in a long portrait, and it is easy to hurry past, but the Hebrew poem is deliberate about hands. This woman's hands seek wool and flax and work willingly; her hands hold the distaff; she stretcheth out her hand to the poor; the fruit of her hands is given her in the gates. Proverbs is not describing a hobby. Spinning was the foundation of every garment the household wore and of the fine linen she afterwards sold to the merchant, and the distaff is the homely end of a trade that clothed a family and turned a profit. Scripture honours this without a trace of condescension and without inflating it into a career. It sits between her provision for her household and her open hand to the needy, which is exactly where the Bible habitually places women's work: inside the home, ordered toward the household, and reaching outward from there with real economic weight. The last word of the chapter is not about thread at all. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the staff from which flax or wool is drawn in spinning; used figuratively for the female sex and for women's domestic work.

expand to see more

DISTAFF, n. The staff from which the flax is drawn in spinning.

DISTAFF, n. Figuratively, a woman, or the female sex; as the distaff side of a family.

SPINDLE, n. The pin used in spinning wheels for twisting the thread.

SPIN, v.t. To draw out and twist into threads, either by the hand or machinery.

FLAX, n. A plant whose fibrous bark is manufactured into linen cloth.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:19 — "She layeth her hands to the spindle, and her hands hold the distaff."

Pro 31:13 — "She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands."

Tit 2:5 — "To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed."

Pro 31:30 — "Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised."

Modern Corruption

Domestic labour is treated as a lesser life from which women must be liberated in order to matter, so that Proverbs 31 is read either as oppression or as sentiment; the text itself presents it as skilled, profitable, honoured work with the fear of the LORD at the centre.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors meet on this verse. The first is the modern reading in which the home is a cage and the distaff a symbol of confinement, so that a woman's worth must be established somewhere else before it can be established at all. Proverbs 31 will not support it: the woman buys a field, plants a vineyard, perceives that her merchandise is good, makes fine linen and sells it, and her own works praise her in the gates. That is not a diminished life. The second error runs the other way and sentimentalises the passage into a greeting card, all softness and no ledger, which flatters nobody and drops the flax and the profit and the strong arms out of the picture.

The dictionary holds the creational order the passage assumes. Titus 2 calls the younger women to be keepers at home, and Proverbs 31 shows what a keeper at home actually looked like with a distaff in her hands and merchandise in the market. Headship and submission are not idleness on either side. The passage ends where the argument must end, with the fear of the LORD, because a competent household without it is only a well-run vanity, and the verse says so plainly: favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kiyshowr (H3601), a distaff; pelek (H6418), a spindle or whirl; kaph (H3709), the palm or hand, the recurring word of the passage.

expand to see more

Hebrew kiyshowr (H3601) — a distaff; occurs only at Proverbs 31:19.

Hebrew pelek (H6418) — a whirl or spindle; also a district, from the turning.

Hebrew kaph (H3709) — the hollow hand, the palm; her hands hold the distaff.

Hebrew chephets (H2656) — delight, pleasure; she worketh willingly, with delight of her hands.

Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, ability, worth; the virtuous woman of verse 10 is a woman of chayil.

Usage

"“her hands hold the distaff” — the single occurrence, in the portrait of Proverbs 31."

"“She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands” — the trade behind the thread."

"The distaff as an old figure for the female line of a household."
